Carbon foams were prepared by polymer sponge replication method using polymer sponges as templates.
Electric conductivity of carbon foams increases rapidly with carbonization temperature.
Electric conductivity values studied ranged from 0.02 S/m to 1.03 S/m.
Carbon foams have a low density of approximately 0.45 g/cm³ due to porous macro- and micro-structure.
SEM images show evenly distributed pores about 1.0 mm in size with micro-scale holes in ligaments.
XRD analysis indicates carbon foams have an amorphous carbon structure with weak graphitic peaks.
Radar absorbing performance was measured by free space method over 4-15 GHz frequency range.
At 0.02 S/m conductivity, maximum absorption peak reached 21.57 dB but with narrow bandwidth (~4.13 GHz above 8 dB).
At 0.46 S/m conductivity, absorption exceeded 8 dB over a broad bandwidth of about 5.76 GHz and 6 dB over 10.62 GHz.
At 1.03 S/m conductivity, absorption performance deteriorated with no frequencies exceeding 8 dB absorption.
Increasing conductivity changes dominant electromagnetic behavior from transmission to reflection.
Broad absorbing bandwidth was achieved without any impedance matching design.
Absorption and reflection are complementary; higher reflection reduces absorption.
Carbon foams can be used as lightweight, broad-bandwidth radar absorbing materials.
Carbonization temperature controls graphitization degree, affecting electric conductivity and absorption.
Carbon foams' porous reticulated structure enhances electromagnetic wave interaction.
Samples had fixed thickness of 15 mm and volume fraction of 30% during testing.
The study emphasizes the need to investigate intrinsic electromagnetic loss mechanisms in carbon foams.
Carbon foams show potential to overcome limitations of traditional magnetic and dielectric RAMs.
The broad absorption bandwidth covers the entire measured frequency range of 4-15 GHz.
